definition: To become less intense, severe, or widespread.
examples: We waited in the cabin for the storm to abate before driving home.
Her anger began to abate once she heard the full story.
etymology: From Old French abatre, 'to beat down', from Latin ab- + battuere 'to beat'.

definition: A departure from what is normal, expected, or typical, often a temporary one.
examples: The cold week in July was an aberration in an otherwise hot summer.
Scientists treated the odd reading as an aberration until it appeared again.
etymology: From Latin aberrare, 'to wander away', from ab- 'away' + errare 'to wander'.

definition: The act of denying oneself pleasures or rights, often for a belief or cause.
examples: The monk's life of abnegation left him with few possessions and fewer comforts.
Her abnegation of personal ambition allowed the whole team to succeed.
etymology: From Latin abnegatio, 'denial', from abnegare, 'to refuse, deny'.

definition: Sparing in eating and drinking; moderate in indulging in pleasures.
examples: The abstemious host served only water and plain bread at the feast.
He led an abstemious life, avoiding sweets, alcohol, and late nights.
etymology: From Latin abstemius, 'temperate', from abs- 'away from' + temetum 'strong drink'.

definition: Difficult to understand because it is deep, complex, or obscure.
examples: The professor's abstruse lecture on quantum field theory baffled even the graduate students.
She avoided abstruse jargon so that every reader could follow her argument.
etymology: From Latin abstrusus, 'hidden', from abstrudere, 'to conceal, thrust away'.

definition: To accept or agree to something reluctantly, without protest.
examples: After hours of argument, the board finally decided to acquiesce to the union's demands.
He would rather acquiesce than start another fight about the thermostat.
etymology: From Latin acquiescere, 'to rest, find repose in', from ad- + quiescere 'to be quiet'.

definition: Bitter, angry feeling or harsh, resentful language, especially in a dispute.
examples: The divorce proceedings were marked by acrimony from the very first meeting.
Despite the acrimony of the campaign, the two rivals shook hands afterward.
etymology: From Latin acrimonia, 'sharpness, pungency', from acer, 'sharp'.

definition: Very skilled and capable at something that takes practice.
examples: She is adept at calming nervous clients before important presentations begin.
After years of travel, he became adept at packing everything into one small bag.
etymology: From Latin adeptus, 'having attained', the past participle of adipisci 'to attain'.

definition: To scold someone gently but firmly, or to warn them earnestly.
examples: The teacher did admonish the class to stop talking during the exam.
My doctor will admonish me again if I skip my walks.
etymology: From Old French amonester, from Latin admonere, 'to warn', from ad- + monere 'to advise'.

definition: To outline roughly or hint at something that will come.
examples: The memo seemed to adumbrate sweeping changes to the company's structure.
Early clouds adumbrate the storm that will hit by evening.
etymology: From Latin adumbrare, 'to shade in, sketch', from umbra, 'shadow'.

definition: Friendly, easy to talk to, and pleasant in manner.
examples: The affable shop owner greeted every customer by name and asked about their families.
His affable personality made him an instant favorite among the new employees.
etymology: From Latin affabilis, 'easy to speak to', from affari 'to speak to'.

definition: Cheerful readiness and eagerness to act or respond quickly.
examples: She accepted the invitation with alacrity and was packed within the hour.
The staff responded with alacrity when the manager asked for volunteers.
etymology: From Latin alacritas, from alacer, 'lively, eager'.

definition: Open to more than one interpretation; not clear in meaning.
examples: The contract's wording was ambiguous, so each side read it differently.
The film ends on an ambiguous note, leaving viewers to decide what really happened.
etymology: From Latin ambiguus, 'doubtful', from ambigere, 'to wander about, be uncertain'.

definition: Having mixed or conflicting feelings about something or someone.
examples: I feel ambivalent about moving, excited about the job but sad to leave my friends.
Voters seemed ambivalent about the proposal and split almost evenly.
etymology: From Latin ambi- 'both' + valentia, 'strength', coined in early 20th-century psychology.

definition: To make a bad or difficult situation better.
examples: New funding should ameliorate the shortage of nurses in rural clinics.
Planting trees can ameliorate the heat in crowded city neighborhoods.
etymology: From French améliorer, from Old French meillor, 'better', from Latin melior.

definition: Having a friendly, good-natured, and agreeable disposition.
examples: Our neighbors are amiable people who always wave and offer to help with the garden.
The two rivals had an amiable chat after the match despite the tense final.
etymology: From Late Latin amicabilis, 'friendly', from Latin amicus 'friend'.

definition: Something out of place in time, especially something that belongs to an earlier era.
examples: A wristwatch in a film about ancient Rome would be an anachronism.
Some critics call the monarchy an anachronism in a modern democracy.
etymology: From Greek anakhronismos, from ana- 'against' + khronos 'time'.

definition: Something or someone strongly disliked or detested.
examples: Waste of any kind is anathema to the thrifty chef.
Compromise was anathema to the party's hardliners, who wanted total victory.
etymology: From Greek anathema, 'a thing devoted, accursed', later used for ecclesiastical curses.

definition: A short, amusing or interesting story about a real person or event.
examples: He opened his speech with an anecdote about his first day on the job.
Grandpa's favorite anecdote involves a goat, a wedding, and a lost hat.
etymology: From Greek anekdota, 'things unpublished', from an- 'not' + ekdotos 'given out'.

definition: Something that deviates from what is standard, normal, or expected.
examples: The data contained one anomaly that the team could not explain.
A warm day in January is an anomaly in this part of the country.
etymology: From Greek anomalos, 'uneven, irregular', from an- 'not' + homalos 'even'.

definition: Extremely old-fashioned or outdated, as if from before the biblical Flood.
examples: His antediluvian computer took ten minutes just to open a spreadsheet.
The club's antediluvian rules still banned women from the main dining room.
etymology: From Latin ante- 'before' + diluvium 'flood'.

definition: The direct opposite of something, or a contrast between two ideas.
examples: His quiet, careful style is the antithesis of his brother's loud showmanship.
The poem sets youth against age, making each the antithesis of the other.
etymology: From Greek antithesis, 'opposition', from anti- 'against' + tithenai 'to place'.

definition: A lack of interest, enthusiasm, or concern about things that matter.
examples: Voter apathy meant that fewer than a quarter of residents turned out.
Years of failure had left the team in a state of apathy.
etymology: From Greek apatheia, 'freedom from suffering', from a- 'without' + pathos 'feeling'.

definition: Calm self-confidence and poise in a difficult or stressful situation.
examples: She handled the surprise question with aplomb and never lost her smile.
The waiter recovered from the spilled tray with remarkable aplomb.
etymology: From French aplomb, 'perpendicularity', from à plomb, 'according to the plumb line'.

definition: Widely told as true but probably invented or of doubtful origin.
examples: The story that he wrote the song in ten minutes is probably apocryphal.
Many apocryphal quotes get credited to Mark Twain or Einstein.
etymology: From Greek apokruphos, 'hidden, obscure', from apo- 'away' + kruptein 'to hide'.

definition: The highest or most perfect example, or the raising of someone to godlike status.
examples: The film was the apotheosis of the director's career, praised by every critic.
Ancient emperors sometimes sought apotheosis, hoping to be worshipped as gods after death.
etymology: From Greek apotheosis, 'deification', from apotheoun, 'to deify'.

definition: Warm praise or official approval, especially from someone in authority.
examples: The plan won the approbation of the committee after a short discussion.
She glowed with the teacher's approbation after reading her poem aloud.
etymology: From Latin approbatio, from approbare, 'to approve'.

definition: Based on random choice or personal whim rather than reason or system.
examples: The deadline seemed arbitrary, since nothing special happened on that date.
Judges should not make arbitrary decisions that ignore the evidence.
etymology: From Latin arbitrarius, 'depending on the will of an arbiter', from arbiter, 'judge'.

definition: Understood by few; mysterious or secret in nature.
examples: The arcane rules of cricket confused the visiting tourists, who gave up halfway through.
He studied arcane texts on alchemy in the dusty library basement.
etymology: From Latin arcanus, 'hidden, secret', from arca, 'chest'.

definition: Showing intense passion, enthusiasm, or devotion.
examples: He was an ardent supporter of the local team, attending every home game.
Her ardent belief in the cause carried her through years of setbacks.
etymology: From Latin ardens, 'burning', from ardere, 'to burn'.

definition: Requiring great effort and endurance; very difficult and tiring.
examples: The arduous climb to the summit took nearly nine hours in freezing wind.
Writing a doctoral thesis is an arduous process that tests even the most patient students.
etymology: From Latin arduus, meaning 'steep' or 'difficult'.

definition: Showing steady, careful, and persistent effort.
examples: Years of assiduous practice finally earned her a seat in the orchestra.
The assiduous clerk checked every figure twice before filing the report.
etymology: From Latin assiduus, 'constantly present', from assidere, 'to sit by'.

definition: To ease or soothe something unpleasant, such as pain, fear, or guilt.
examples: A warm drink might assuage your sore throat tonight.
The mayor tried to assuage public fears about the new factory.
etymology: From Old French assouagier, from Latin ad- 'to' + suavis 'sweet, pleasant'.

definition: Quick to see how a situation works and use it to advantage.
examples: An astute investor, she sold her shares just before the market began to fall.
The astute detective noticed that the muddy footprints led away from the open window.
etymology: From Latin astutus, 'crafty, shrewd', from astus 'cunning'.

definition: Relating to a primitive instinct or trait inherited from distant ancestors.
examples: He felt an atavistic urge to flee when he heard the low growl.
The crowd's atavistic fear of the dark showed as the lights went out.
etymology: From Latin atavus, 'ancestor', literally a great-great-great-grandfather.

definition: Boldly daring, willing to take surprising risks.
examples: The startup made an audacious plan to deliver groceries by drone to remote villages.
It was an audacious move to ask the CEO for a raise on his first day.
etymology: From Latin audax, 'bold', from audere 'to dare'.

definition: Suggesting that future success is likely; favorable.
examples: Sunny skies made for an auspicious start to the festival.
It was not an auspicious debut, since the lead actor forgot his lines.
etymology: From Latin auspicium, 'divination by watching birds', from avis 'bird' + specere 'to look'.

definition: Plain, severe, and strict, with no comfort or decoration.
examples: The monks lived in an austere stone building with only a bed and a candle.
Her austere style of leadership left little room for jokes or informal chats.
etymology: From Greek austeros, 'harsh, dry', via Old French and Latin.

definition: Extreme greed for wealth or material gain.
examples: The novel's villain is driven by avarice and will betray anyone for gold.
Critics accused the executives of avarice after they awarded themselves huge bonuses.
etymology: From Latin avaritia, from avarus, 'greedy', from avere, 'to crave'.

definition: Lacking originality and so ordinary that it is boring.
examples: The speech was full of banal phrases like 'think outside the box'.
Small talk about the weather can feel banal, yet it breaks the ice.
etymology: From French banal, originally 'shared by tenants of a feudal estate', hence commonplace.

definition: Eager to fight; aggressive and warlike in manner.
examples: The bellicose general demanded immediate action against the neighboring state.
His bellicose speech alarmed diplomats who had hoped for peaceful talks.
etymology: From Latin bellicosus, 'warlike', from bellum, 'war'.

definition: Hostile and aggressive, eager to fight or argue.
examples: The belligerent customer shouted at the staff until security arrived.
Tensions rose when the neighboring country adopted a belligerent tone.
etymology: From Latin belligerare, 'to wage war', from bellum 'war' + gerere 'to carry on'.

definition: Kind and generous, wanting to do good for other people.
examples: A benevolent donor paid off the medical debts of hundreds of local families.
The king was remembered as a benevolent ruler who built schools and hospitals.
etymology: From Latin bene 'well' + volens 'wishing', from velle 'to wish'.

definition: Gentle and harmless, or (of a growth) not cancerous.
examples: The doctor said the lump was benign and needed no treatment.
He had a benign smile that put nervous patients at ease.
etymology: From Latin benignus, 'kind', from bene 'well' + genus 'born, kind'.

definition: Completely obvious and done openly, without any attempt to hide it.
examples: The referee ignored a blatant foul right in front of him.
It was a blatant lie, and everyone in the room knew it.
etymology: Coined by Edmund Spenser in 1596 for a monstrous beast; later extended to mean 'obvious'.

definition: To support or strengthen something, making it more secure or effective.
examples: New evidence helped bolster her argument that the bridge was unsafe.
A strong cup of coffee did little to bolster my courage before the interview.
etymology: From Old English bolster, 'a long cushion or pillow'; the verb sense means to prop up.

definition: Using grand, inflated language that sounds impressive but means little.
examples: The candidate's bombastic speech promised everything and explained nothing.
He wrote in a bombastic style, piling up long words to sound important.
etymology: From bombast, from Old French bombace, 'cotton padding', hence padded or inflated speech.

definition: The quality of using few words or lasting only a short time.
examples: The brevity of her speech surprised the audience, who expected an hour of remarks.
Poets often prize brevity, packing a whole feeling into just a few lines.
etymology: From Latin brevitas, from brevis 'short'.

definition: Pleasantly rural or pastoral, like idealized countryside life.
examples: They retired to a bucolic village surrounded by meadows and grazing sheep.
The painting captured a bucolic scene of farmers resting beneath an oak tree.
etymology: From Greek boukolikos, 'of herdsmen', from boukolos, 'cowherd'.

definition: To grow or increase rapidly; to flourish.
examples: The city's food scene continues to burgeon, with new restaurants opening weekly.
Wildflowers burgeon across the hills each April after the winter rains.
etymology: From Old French burjon, 'bud, shoot', possibly of Germanic origin.

definition: A harsh, jarring mixture of loud and unpleasant sounds.
examples: A cacophony of car horns greeted us as we left the station.
The kindergarten band produced a cacophony of banging, honking, and giggles.
etymology: From Greek kakophonia, from kakos 'bad' + phone 'sound'.

definition: To persuade someone to do something through flattery or gentle coaxing.
examples: She managed to cajole her brother into driving her to the airport.
Salespeople often cajole shoppers with compliments and small discounts.
etymology: From French cajoler, 'to chatter like a jay, coax', of uncertain origin.

definition: Showing no sympathy or concern for the feelings of others.
examples: His callous remark about the layoffs shocked everyone in the room.
Years in the emergency room had not made her callous toward suffering.
etymology: From Latin callosus, 'hard-skinned', from callum, 'hard skin'.

definition: Young and inexperienced, lacking maturity or worldly knowledge.
examples: The callow intern confidently offered advice to executives with thirty years of experience.
Looking back, she cringed at her callow belief that success would come easily.
etymology: From Old English calu, 'bald', later meaning unfledged, hence immature.

definition: Honest and direct in speech, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
examples: Thank you for being candid about the problems with my draft before I submitted it.
The actor gave a candid interview about his struggles early in his career.
etymology: From Latin candidus, 'white, pure, sincere', from candere 'to shine'.

definition: Honest, open, and sincere expression, even when the truth is uncomfortable.
examples: I appreciated her candor when she said the first draft was weak.
He spoke with refreshing candor about his mistakes as a young manager.
etymology: From Latin candor, 'whiteness, sincerity', from candere, 'to shine, be white'.

definition: Given to sudden, unpredictable changes of mood or behavior.
examples: The capricious weather ruined our picnic plans three weekends in a row.
A capricious boss can make it impossible to know what is expected.
etymology: From Italian capriccio, 'sudden start, whim', perhaps literally 'shiver' or 'goat leap'.

definition: Tending to find fault and raise petty objections.
examples: The captious critic pounced on every tiny error in the otherwise fine film.
Her captious questions seemed designed to trap the speaker, not to learn.
etymology: From Latin captiosus, 'sophistical, deceptive', from capere, 'to take'.

definition: To criticize or reprimand someone severely.
examples: The press did castigate the senator for ignoring the report's warnings.
Coaches shouldn't castigate young players for honest mistakes.
etymology: From Latin castigare, 'to correct, punish', from castus 'pure' + agere 'to drive'.

definition: A person or event that triggers important change or action.
examples: The scandal became the catalyst for a complete overhaul of the agency.
Her speech was the catalyst that finally got the neighbors organized.
etymology: From Greek katalysis, 'dissolution', from kata- 'down' + lysis 'loosening'; the chemistry sense came first.

definition: Bitingly sarcastic, or capable of burning and corroding by chemical action.
examples: The critic's caustic review left the director furious for weeks.
Wear gloves when handling caustic cleaners, because they can burn skin.
etymology: From Greek kaustikos, 'capable of burning', from kaiein, 'to burn'.

definition: A feeling of annoyed disappointment or embarrassment after a failure or mistake.
examples: To her chagrin, she realized she had been wearing mismatched shoes all day.
He read the error message with chagrin, knowing he had deleted the wrong file.
etymology: From French chagrin, 'sorrow, distress', possibly from chagrin 'rough leather'.

definition: Clever trickery or deception, especially in legal or political matters.
examples: The contract was riddled with legal chicanery meant to cheat small investors.
He won the election through chicanery, including fake endorsements and false rumors.
etymology: From French chicanerie, from chicaner, 'to quibble', of uncertain origin.

definition: Imaginary or wildly unrealistic; existing only as a fanciful dream.
examples: Her chimerical plans for a floating city never left the sketchbook.
The investors dismissed the idea as chimerical, with no basis in real technology.
etymology: From Chimera, the fire-breathing monster of Greek myth, with the suffix -ical.

definition: Rude, mean-spirited, and ill-mannered, especially in refusing to be gracious.
examples: It would be churlish to refuse a gift offered so kindly.
His churlish reply to the waiter embarrassed everyone at the table.
etymology: From Old English ceorl, 'a peasant, free man of low rank', plus -ish.

definition: The use of many words to say something that could be said simply.
examples: The politician's circumlocution avoided the question without ever refusing to answer it.
After a long circumlocution, he finally admitted that he had forgotten the report.
etymology: From Latin circumlocutio, from circum- 'around' + loqui 'to speak'.

definition: Careful to consider possible consequences before acting or speaking.
examples: Be circumspect about what you post online, since employers may read it.
The diplomat was circumspect, offering no comment until all the facts were known.
etymology: From Latin circumspectus, 'looked around', from circum 'around' + specere 'to look'.

definition: Kept secret, often because the activity is illegal or forbidden.
examples: The two leaders held a clandestine meeting in a hotel basement.
They ran a clandestine radio station from an abandoned farmhouse.
etymology: From Latin clandestinus, 'secret, hidden', from clam, 'secretly'.

definition: Unpleasantly sweet or sentimental to the point of disgust.
examples: The cloying perfume filled the elevator and left everyone wincing.
Critics found the film's cloying romance too sugary to enjoy.
etymology: From cloy, from Middle English acloyen, 'to nail up, clog', from Latin clavus, 'nail'.

definition: Clear, logical, and convincing.
examples: She made a cogent case for moving the launch to autumn.
The lawyer's cogent argument persuaded even the skeptical jurors.
etymology: From Latin cogens, 'compelling', from cogere, 'to drive together, force'.

definition: Logical and well organized, so that all the parts fit together clearly.
examples: After the shock, he was barely coherent and could not explain what had happened.
A coherent argument moves step by step from evidence to a clear conclusion.
etymology: From Latin cohaerere, 'to stick together', from co- 'together' + haerere 'to stick'.

definition: Matching in size, amount, or importance; proportionate.
examples: Salary will be commensurate with experience, according to the job posting.
The punishment should be commensurate with the seriousness of the offense.
etymology: From Late Latin commensuratus, from com- 'together' + mensurare 'to measure'.

definition: Smugly satisfied with how things are, and so careless about possible problems.
examples: The champions grew complacent after three easy wins and were stunned by a late defeat.
Don't get complacent about your health just because you feel fine today.
etymology: From Latin complacere, 'to please greatly', from com- + placere 'to please'.

definition: Involved with others in wrongdoing, even if only by staying silent.
examples: Anyone who knew about the fraud and stayed silent was complicit.
The company was complicit in hiding the safety defects from regulators.
etymology: From Late Latin complex, 'closely connected', from com- 'together' + plicare 'to fold'.

definition: A pang of guilt or uneasiness about doing something wrong.
examples: He lied to his clients without compunction and slept soundly each night.
She felt a flicker of compunction as she deleted her sister's message.
etymology: From Latin compunctio, 'a pricking', from compungere, 'to prick sharply'.

definition: Giving a lot of information clearly in very few words.
examples: Her concise summary captured the whole report in just three sentences.
Keep your emails concise so busy colleagues will actually read them to the end.
etymology: From Latin concisus, 'cut short', from concidere 'to cut off'.

definition: Making a certain good result easy or likely to happen.
examples: A quiet room with soft light is conducive to deep sleep.
The open office was not conducive to concentration, so many people wore headphones.
etymology: From Latin conducere, 'to lead together', from con- + ducere 'to lead'.

definition: A large, destructive fire that spreads widely.
examples: A small spark grew into a conflagration that swept across the dry hills.
The Great Fire of London was a conflagration that destroyed much of the city.
etymology: From Latin conflagratio, from conflagrare, 'to burn up', from com- + flagrare 'to blaze'.

definition: An opinion or conclusion formed from incomplete information rather than proof.
examples: Whether the ruins were a temple is pure conjecture, since no records survive.
Her theory remains conjecture until someone can test it.
etymology: From Latin coniectura, 'a throwing together', from conicere, 'to infer, throw together'.

definition: A person with expert knowledge and refined taste in an art, food, or drink.
examples: As a coffee connoisseur, he can tell the roast's origin by smell alone.
The gallery owner is a true connoisseur of early photography.
etymology: From French connoisseur, from Old French connoistre, 'to know', from Latin cognoscere.

definition: Careful and thorough, taking great care to do tasks properly.
examples: A conscientious student, he rechecked every answer before handing in the exam.
The conscientious nurse documented each change in the patient's condition without fail.
etymology: From Latin conscientia, 'knowledge, moral sense', from conscire 'to be aware'.

definition: Stubbornly disobedient, especially toward authority or a court.
examples: The contumacious witness refused again to answer the judge's questions.
His contumacious attitude toward every rule got him expelled from school.
etymology: From Latin contumax, 'stubborn, insolent', of uncertain origin.

definition: A confusing problem or puzzling question with no easy answer.
examples: Choosing between a higher salary and a shorter commute is a real conundrum.
The mystery of the missing keys remained a conundrum until we checked the freezer.
etymology: Of unknown origin; first appeared in 17th-century English as a slang word, possibly a joke.

definition: Existing in large amounts; plentiful.
examples: She took copious notes during the lecture and filled half a notebook.
The recipe calls for copious amounts of garlic.
etymology: From Latin copiosus, 'plentiful', from copia, 'abundance'.

definition: Warm, polite, and friendly in a sincere but often formal way.
examples: The two leaders shared a cordial handshake before the talks began.
She sent a cordial invitation to every neighbor on the street.
etymology: From Medieval Latin cordialis, 'of the heart', from Latin cor 'heart'.

definition: To confirm or support a statement or finding with additional evidence.
examples: Two independent witnesses were able to corroborate her account of the accident.
Later studies did corroborate the original findings.
etymology: From Latin corroborare, 'to strengthen', from com- + roborare 'to make strong', from robur 'strength'.

definition: Able to be believed or trusted because it seems reasonable.
examples: The witness gave a credible account that matched the security camera footage.
Without a credible source, the rumor should not be shared online.
etymology: From Latin credibilis, from credere 'to believe'.

definition: Having a hidden or puzzling meaning that is hard to understand.
examples: He left a cryptic note on the fridge that no one could decode.
Her cryptic smile gave no hint of whether she approved of the plan.
etymology: From Late Latin crypticus, from Greek kryptos, 'hidden'.

definition: To reach a final high point or result after a long process.
examples: The long negotiations will culminate in a signing ceremony next Friday.
Months of training culminate in a single race on Sunday morning.
etymology: From Late Latin culminare, 'to crown', from Latin culmen 'peak, summit'.

definition: Deserving blame or responsibility for a fault or wrongdoing.
examples: The court found the driver culpable for the crash because he was texting.
I feel partly culpable, since I knew about the problem and said nothing.
etymology: From Latin culpabilis, from culpa, 'fault, blame'.

definition: To develop or improve something, such as a skill, habit, or relationship, with care.
examples: She tried to cultivate patience by meditating for ten minutes each morning.
Good managers cultivate trust long before a crisis arrives.
etymology: From Medieval Latin cultivare, 'to till', from Latin cultus, past participle of colere, 'to tend, till'.

definition: Strong greed for money or possessions.
examples: The king's cupidity drove him to tax his people until they had nothing left.
Their cupidity blinded them to the obvious risks of the get-rich-quick scheme.
etymology: From Latin cupiditas, 'passionate desire', from cupidus, 'desirous', from cupere, 'to desire'.

definition: Done quickly and without attention to detail.
examples: A cursory glance at the report was enough to spot several errors.
The inspector gave the building only a cursory check before signing off.
etymology: From Latin cursorius, 'of a runner', from cursor, 'runner', from currere, 'to run'.

definition: A scarcity or lack of something that is needed.
examples: The town's dearth of affordable housing pushed many young families to move away.
A dearth of good ideas left the writers staring at a blank board.
etymology: From Middle English derthe, 'costliness, scarcity', related to dear.

definition: A sudden and total failure that causes embarrassment or chaos.
examples: The product launch was a debacle, with the website crashing within minutes.
After the debacle at the final, the coach resigned the next morning.
etymology: From French débâcle, 'breaking up of ice in a river', from débâcler 'to unbar'.

definition: To make someone or something seriously weak or unable to function well.
examples: A long bout of the flu can debilitate even the healthiest athlete.
Constant budget cuts began to debilitate the once-proud public library system.
etymology: From Latin debilitare, 'to weaken', from debilis 'weak'.

definition: Polite, proper behavior that suits a formal or serious occasion.
examples: The judge demanded decorum and warned the crowd to stop shouting.
She kept her decorum even when the dinner conversation turned rude.
etymology: From Latin decorum, 'what is fitting', from decor 'beauty, grace'.

definition: To throw someone or something out of a window.
examples: The enraged rock star threatened to defenestrate the hotel television.
Historians recall how rebels chose to defenestrate the royal officials in Prague in 1618.
etymology: From Latin de- 'out of' + fenestra 'window'.

definition: Polite respect shown by yielding to another person's wishes or opinion.
examples: The young lawyer spoke with deference to the senior judge.
In deference to her grandmother, she changed out of her ripped jeans.
etymology: From French déférence, from déférer 'to yield', from Latin deferre 'to carry away'.

definition: Quick, neat, and skillful in movement or handling a situation.
examples: With a deft flick of the wrist, the chef flipped the omelet.
She gave a deft answer that avoided the trap hidden in the question.
etymology: From Middle English deft, a variant of 'daft' in its older sense 'gentle, fitting'.

definition: Causing harm or damage, often in a gradual or subtle way.
examples: Years of poor sleep can have a deleterious effect on your memory.
The chemical spill had deleterious consequences for the river's fish.
etymology: From Greek deleterios, 'harmful', from deleisthai 'to harm'.

definition: To melt away or dissolve gradually, especially by absorbing moisture from the air.
examples: Salt left in the damp cellar began to deliquesce into a sticky puddle.
By evening, her careful plans began to deliquesce into confusion.
etymology: From Latin deliquescere, 'to melt away', from de- + liquescere 'to become liquid'.

definition: To dig deeply into a subject to find more information.
examples: Let's delve into the data to see why sales dropped in March.
The documentary delves into the hidden history of the old harbor.
etymology: From Old English delfan, meaning 'to dig'.

definition: A political leader who stirs up emotions and prejudices to gain power.
examples: The demagogue whipped up the crowd with promises he could never keep.
Voters should be wary of any demagogue who blames every problem on a single group.
etymology: From Greek demagogos, 'leader of the people', from demos 'people' + agogos 'leader'.

definition: Modest, quiet, and reserved in manner, often in a shy way.
examples: She gave a demure smile and said nothing about her award.
The demure student surprised everyone by delivering a fiery speech.
etymology: From Middle English, probably from Old French demore, 'settled, grave'.

definition: To mock or laugh at someone or something with contempt.
examples: Critics were quick to deride the film as shallow and predictable.
It is cruel to deride a colleague for asking an honest question.
etymology: From Latin deridere, 'to laugh to scorn', from de- + ridere 'to laugh'.

definition: Feeling deep discouragement and loss of hope.
examples: He grew despondent after months of job rejections with no replies.
The team sat despondent in the locker room after the final whistle.
etymology: From Latin despondere, 'to give up, lose heart', from de- + spondere 'to promise'.

definition: Lacking a plan or enthusiasm; jumping from one thing to another.
examples: They made desultory conversation while waiting for the late train.
His desultory efforts at studying did nothing to improve his grades.
etymology: From Latin desultorius, 'of a leaper', from desilire, 'to jump down'.

definition: To discourage someone from acting by making them fear the consequences.
examples: Bright lights around the house deter burglars from trying to break in.
Bad weather did not deter the crowds from lining up for the concert.
etymology: From Latin deterrere, 'to frighten away', from de- 'away' + terrere 'to frighten'.

definition: Light, delicate, and so thin that it is nearly see-through.
examples: She wore a diaphanous scarf that fluttered in the summer breeze.
Morning mist hung over the lake in a diaphanous veil.
etymology: From Greek diaphanes, 'transparent', from dia- 'through' + phainein 'to show'.

definition: A long, bitter verbal attack or angry speech against someone or something.
examples: His diatribe against the new parking rules lasted a full twenty minutes.
The comment section filled with one long diatribe about the company's decisions.
etymology: From Greek diatribe, 'a wearing away of time', later 'a discourse'.

definition: Intended to teach, often in an overly preachy or moralizing way.
examples: The novel felt didactic, with every chapter ending in a neat lesson.
Her didactic tone made friends reluctant to ask her for advice.
etymology: From Greek didaktikos, 'apt at teaching', from didaskein 'to teach'.

definition: Lacking self-confidence and hesitant to speak or act boldly.
examples: The diffident intern rarely shared ideas, though many were excellent.
He gave a diffident shrug and quietly slipped out of the spotlight.
etymology: From Latin diffidere, 'to mistrust', from dis- 'apart' + fidere 'to trust'.

definition: To wander away from the main topic while speaking or writing.
examples: Forgive me if I digress, but this reminds me of my trip to Peru.
Professors often digress into stories that students end up remembering best.
etymology: From Latin digredi, 'to step aside', from di- 'apart' + gradi 'to step'.

definition: A person who dabbles in a subject without serious commitment or deep knowledge.
examples: He was a dilettante who tried painting, then pottery, then violin, mastering none.
Experts dismissed the critic as a dilettante with opinions but no real training.
etymology: From Italian dilettante, 'lover of the arts', from dilettare, 'to delight'.

definition: Showing steady, careful effort in whatever one does.
examples: A diligent worker, she finished every task well before the deadline.
Thanks to diligent practice, his piano playing improved dramatically over one year.
etymology: From Latin diligens, 'attentive', from diligere 'to esteem, love'.

definition: To notice or recognize something that is not immediately obvious.
examples: In the dim light, I could barely discern the outline of a boat.
It takes experience to discern a genuine antique from a clever copy.
etymology: From Latin discernere, 'to separate', from dis- 'apart' + cernere 'to sift'.

definition: Not sincere; pretending to know less or be more honest than one is.
examples: It was disingenuous of him to act surprised when he had planned everything.
Her disingenuous apology sounded more like a way to protect herself.
etymology: From dis- 'not' + ingenuous, from Latin ingenuus, 'freeborn, candid'.

definition: Gloomy and depressing, or very poor in quality.
examples: The dismal weather kept everyone indoors for the whole week.
The team's dismal performance left fans heading for the exits before halftime.
etymology: From Anglo-French dis mal, from Latin dies mali, 'evil days'.

definition: So different in kind that the things cannot be easily compared or combined.
examples: The festival brought together disparate groups who rarely spoke to each other.
She wove disparate ideas from music and biology into a single theory.
etymology: From Latin disparatus, 'separated', influenced by dispar 'unequal'.

definition: To hide your true feelings or intentions behind a false appearance.
examples: The suspect tried to dissemble, smiling calmly while hiding his panic.
Politicians who dissemble about their plans quickly lose the voters' trust.
etymology: From Old French dessembler, altered under the influence of Latin dis- + simulare 'to pretend'.

definition: A harsh clash of sounds, or a lack of agreement between ideas.
examples: The orchestra ended on a tense dissonance that left the audience unsettled.
There was real dissonance between what the CEO promised and what employees saw.
etymology: From Latin dissonare, 'to sound harshly', from dis- + sonare 'to sound'.

definition: Stating opinions as undeniable truth and refusing to consider other views.
examples: His dogmatic approach to diet made every dinner party an argument.
A good scientist avoids being dogmatic and updates beliefs when new evidence appears.
etymology: From Greek dogma, 'opinion, belief', from dokein 'to seem good'.

definition: Doubtful or suspect; not fully trusted or likely to be good.
examples: I am dubious about any diet that promises results in three days.
He earned his money through dubious business deals that regulators later investigated.
etymology: From Latin dubiosus, 'doubtful', from dubium 'doubt'.

definition: Deceitful behavior in which a person says one thing but does another.
examples: The duplicity of his business partner came to light after the audit.
She was shocked by the duplicity of a friend who smiled and lied.
etymology: From Latin duplicitas, 'doubleness', from duplex 'twofold'.

definition: To become gradually smaller, weaker, or fewer over time.
examples: Our food supplies began to dwindle after the third week at sea.
Interest in the club will dwindle if meetings stay this dull.
etymology: Probably from Old English dwinan, 'to shrink, waste away', with a frequentative suffix.

definition: Serious and sincere, with real and heartfelt intensity.
examples: He made an earnest apology and promised to repair the damage himself.
The earnest young volunteer spent every weekend cleaning the river bank.
etymology: From Old English eornost, meaning 'seriousness, zeal'.

definition: Overflowing with cheerful energy and enthusiasm.
examples: The ebullient coach hugged every player after the unexpected win.
Her ebullient laugh filled the room and lifted everyone's mood.
etymology: From Latin ebullire, 'to bubble up', from e- 'out' + bullire 'to boil'.

definition: Drawing on a wide mix of styles, sources, or tastes.
examples: Her eclectic playlist ranges from jazz and opera to punk rock.
The cafe has an eclectic look, with mismatched chairs and old posters.
etymology: From Greek eklektikos, 'selective', from eklegein 'to pick out'.

definition: To instruct or uplift someone morally or intellectually.
examples: The museum aims to edify visitors, not just entertain them.
She chose books that would edify her children as well as amuse them.
etymology: From Latin aedificare, 'to build', from aedes 'building' + facere 'to make'.

definition: The ability of something to produce the intended result.
examples: Trials confirmed the efficacy of the new vaccine against severe illness.
Few people doubt the efficacy of a good night's sleep before an exam.
etymology: From Latin efficacia, from efficax 'effective', from efficere 'to accomplish'.

definition: Shameless boldness or rudeness that disregards what is proper.
examples: He had the effrontery to ask for a raise after missing the deadline.
Her effrontery shocked the guests when she corrected the host in public.
etymology: From French effronterie, from Late Latin effrons, 'shameless', from ex- + frons 'forehead'.

definition: Expressing feelings in an unrestrained, gushing way.
examples: He was effusive in his thanks, repeating them again at the door.
The reviewer was effusive about the debut novel and called it a masterpiece.
etymology: From Latin effusus, 'poured out', from effundere 'to pour forth'.

definition: Shockingly bad and obvious, standing out in a negative way.
examples: The newspaper printed a correction for an egregious error in the headline.
Ignoring the safety warnings was an egregious failure of leadership.
etymology: From Latin egregius, 'outstanding', literally 'standing out from the herd'.

definition: Detailed and complicated, with many carefully arranged parts.
examples: They planned an elaborate surprise party with a live band and fireworks.
The spy devised an elaborate scheme involving three false names.
etymology: From Latin elaboratus, 'worked out', from e- 'out' + laborare 'to work'.

definition: Extremely happy and excited, often because of a success.
examples: She was elated when she opened the letter and saw the acceptance.
The crowd was elated as the winning goal sailed into the net.
etymology: From Latin elatus, 'lifted up', past participle of efferre 'to raise'.

definition: To draw out a response, reaction, or piece of information from someone.
examples: The comedian's joke failed to elicit even a single laugh.
Careful questions helped the nurse elicit a full account of the symptoms.
etymology: From Latin elicere, 'to draw out', from e- 'out' + lacere 'to entice'.

definition: Able to speak or write in a fluent, persuasive, and moving way.
examples: The eloquent speaker held the whole auditorium in silence for nearly an hour.
Her letter was short but eloquent, and it changed the council's mind.
etymology: From Latin eloquens, 'speaking out', from eloqui 'to speak out'.

definition: Hard to find, catch, or remember; always slipping away.
examples: The elusive snow leopard is rarely seen, even by local guides.
Sleep remained elusive, and he lay awake until the sun came up.
etymology: From Latin eludere, 'to escape or deceive', from e- 'out' + ludere 'to play'.

definition: To begin a journey or start a major new project.
examples: They will embark on a six-month trip around the world next spring.
Before you embark on a renovation, set a realistic budget.
etymology: From French embarquer, from Latin in- 'in' + barca 'small ship'.

definition: To make something more attractive or interesting by adding details, often untrue ones.
examples: Grandpa liked to embellish his fishing stories with ever larger fish.
The chef will embellish each plate with a sprig of fresh herbs.
etymology: From Old French embellir, 'to make beautiful', from bel 'beautiful'.

definition: Famous and highly respected, especially in a profession.
examples: An eminent scientist will deliver the opening lecture at the conference.
She became an eminent surgeon known across the country for her skill.
etymology: From Latin eminens, 'standing out', from eminere 'to stand out, project'.

definition: The ability to understand and share another person's feelings.
examples: A good nurse shows empathy for patients who are afraid.
Reading fiction can build empathy by putting you inside someone else's life.
etymology: From Greek empatheia, 'passion', from en- 'in' + pathos 'feeling'; modern sense via German Einfühlung.

definition: Based on observation or experiment rather than on theory alone.
examples: The new study offers empirical evidence that regular exercise improves mood and sleep.
He wanted empirical proof from the lab, not just another persuasive argument.
etymology: From Greek empeirikos, 'experienced', from empeiria 'experience'.

definition: To copy someone admired, trying to equal or surpass them.
examples: Young players try to emulate the champions they watch on television.
She hoped to emulate her mentor's calm and steady leadership style one day.
etymology: From Latin aemulari, 'to rival', from aemulus 'rivaling'.

definition: A speech or writing that warmly praises a person or thing.
examples: The retiring coach received an encomium from the mayor at the ceremony.
His eulogy was an encomium to his teacher's patience and generosity.
etymology: From Latin encomium, from Greek enkomion, 'a song of praise'.

definition: A serious, sustained attempt to achieve something.
examples: Climbing the mountain was a risky endeavor that required months of planning.
Every creative endeavor involves moments of doubt and many rough drafts.
etymology: From Middle English endeveren, 'to put oneself in duty', from French en devoir.

definition: To drain someone of energy and strength.
examples: The summer heat can enervate even the most dedicated hikers.
Hours of pointless meetings tend to enervate the whole team.
etymology: From Latin enervare, 'to weaken', from e- 'out' + nervus 'sinew'.

definition: A person or thing that is mysterious and hard to understand.
examples: The reclusive author remains an enigma to even her closest readers.
How the ancient builders moved those stones is still an enigma.
etymology: From Greek ainigma, 'riddle', from ainissesthai 'to speak in riddles'.

definition: Deep and lasting hostility between people or groups.
examples: Centuries of enmity between the families made peace seem impossible.
There was no enmity in his voice, only quiet disappointment.
etymology: From Old French enemistie, from Latin inimicus, 'enemy'.

definition: Lasting for only a very short time.
examples: Fame on social media can be ephemeral, gone within a week.
The ephemeral beauty of cherry blossoms draws crowds each spring.
etymology: From Greek ephemeros, 'lasting a day', from epi- 'on' + hemera 'day'.

definition: A perfect example that shows all the typical qualities of something.
examples: With her calm grace, she was the epitome of professionalism.
That tiny cottage is the epitome of cozy country living.
etymology: From Greek epitome, 'abridgment', from epitemnein 'to cut short'.

definition: Mental calmness and composure, especially in difficult situations.
examples: She faced the disappointing news with remarkable equanimity and even offered a smile.
Years of meditation gave him the equanimity to stay calm in traffic.
etymology: From Latin aequanimitas, from aequus 'even' + animus 'mind'.

definition: Open to more than one interpretation, and often deliberately unclear.
examples: The senator gave an equivocal answer that pleased neither side.
The test results were equivocal, so the doctor ordered another scan.
etymology: From Latin aequivocus, from aequus 'equal' + vox 'voice'.

definition: To speak vaguely on purpose in order to avoid committing or telling the truth.
examples: The spokesman continued to equivocate when reporters asked about the missing funds.
If you equivocate when asked a simple question, people will suspect you are hiding something.
etymology: From Latin aequivocus, 'having the same sound', from aequus 'equal' + vox 'voice'.

definition: Fake and inferior, made as a substitute for the real thing.
examples: During the shortage, the cafe served ersatz coffee made from roasted barley.
She wore an ersatz fur coat that fooled no one at the party.
etymology: From German Ersatz, 'replacement, substitute'.

definition: To deliberately avoid or abstain from something.
examples: He chose to eschew social media and spend his quiet evenings reading instead.
Many athletes eschew sugary snacks and late nights during the competition season.
etymology: From Old French eschiver, 'to avoid', of Germanic origin.

definition: Understood by only a small group with specialized knowledge.
examples: The professor's esoteric lecture on medieval grammar baffled most of the class.
He collects esoteric records that only a handful of fans have heard.
etymology: From Greek esoterikos, 'inner', from eso 'within'.

definition: A mild or indirect word used in place of a harsh or blunt one.
examples: Passed away is a common euphemism for died, used to soften the news.
The memo used the euphemism restructuring to avoid saying that people would be laid off.
etymology: From Greek euphemismos, from eu 'well' + pheme 'speech'.

definition: Quickly fading or disappearing; lasting only a very short time.
examples: The evanescent beauty of cherry blossoms is part of why people treasure them.
Fame can be evanescent, vanishing as quickly as it arrived.
etymology: From Latin evanescere, 'to vanish', from e- 'out' + vanescere 'to disappear'.

definition: To make a problem or bad situation worse.
examples: Skipping meals and sleep will only exacerbate your headache and make the day harder.
Harsh criticism tends to exacerbate tension rather than solve the underlying problem.
etymology: From Latin exacerbare, 'to irritate', from ex- + acerbus 'harsh, bitter'.

definition: To criticize someone or something very harshly and severely.
examples: Reviewers were quick to excoriate the film for its weak script and wooden acting.
The senator rose to excoriate the committee for ignoring the warning signs.
etymology: From Latin excoriare, 'to strip the skin off', from ex- + corium 'skin, hide'.

definition: Extremely bad; deserving of strong hatred or disgust.
examples: The soup was execrable, tasting of burnt rubber and old dishwater.
His execrable manners ruined what had been a pleasant dinner.
etymology: From Latin execrabilis, from execrari, 'to curse', from ex- + sacer 'sacred'.

definition: Serving as an excellent model worth copying.
examples: Her exemplary conduct as a captain earned the respect of the entire team.
The school received an award for its exemplary record of student support.
etymology: From Latin exemplaris, 'serving as a copy', from exemplum 'example'.

definition: To officially clear someone of blame or wrongdoing.
examples: New DNA evidence helped exonerate the man after ten years in prison.
The investigation did exonerate the pilot of any responsibility for the crash.
etymology: From Latin exonerare, 'to unburden', from ex- + onus 'burden'.

definition: Convenient and practical for a purpose, though not always right or fair.
examples: Cutting corners was expedient, but it cost the company its reputation.
The mayor chose the expedient solution rather than the best long-term fix.
etymology: From Latin expediens, 'freeing the feet', from expedire 'to extricate'.

definition: To make amends for a wrong by suffering or doing penance.
examples: He tried to expiate his guilt by volunteering at the shelter every weekend.
No amount of apology could expiate the harm caused by the lie.
etymology: From Latin expiare, 'to atone for', from ex- + piare 'to appease', from pius 'devout'.

definition: To praise something enthusiastically and at length.
examples: Reviewers continue to extol the novel's vivid characters and its unforgettable final chapter.
My uncle will extol the virtues of cast-iron pans to anyone willing to listen.
etymology: From Latin extollere, 'to lift up', from ex- 'up' + tollere 'to raise'.

definition: Full of lively, joyful energy and enthusiasm.
examples: The exuberant crowd cheered and danced long after the band left the stage.
Her exuberant laugh filled the whole room and made everyone smile.
etymology: From Latin exuberare, 'to be abundant', from ex- 'thoroughly' + uber 'fertile'.

definition: Playfully joking in a way that is not serious, often at the wrong time.
examples: Please do not be facetious; this is a serious matter.
His facetious reply made the class laugh and the teacher frown.
etymology: From French facétieux, from Latin facetia, 'a jest'.

definition: To make a process or action easier or help it run smoothly.
examples: A good teacher will facilitate discussion rather than simply giving a lecture.
New software should facilitate faster communication between the two offices.
etymology: From French faciliter, from Latin facilis 'easy'.

definition: Very careful about details and difficult to please.
examples: The fastidious editor checked every comma twice before finally approving the book for print.
She is fastidious about keeping her desk perfectly organized, down to the last paper clip.
etymology: From Latin fastidiosus, 'disdainful', from fastidium 'loathing'.

definition: Silly and pointless, showing a lack of thought or intelligence.
examples: His fatuous remarks at the meeting wasted everyone's time and lowered their patience.
She wore a fatuous grin while delivering the worst news of the quarter.
etymology: From Latin fatuus, 'foolish, silly'.

definition: Possible to do or achieve in a practical way.
examples: Is it feasible to finish the whole project by the end of the month?
Engineers found a feasible way to bring clean water to the village.
etymology: From Old French faisable, 'doable', from faire 'to do', from Latin facere.

definition: Lacking initiative or responsibility; weak and ineffective.
examples: The feckless manager forgot meetings and blamed his staff for the chaos.
She was tired of her feckless brother borrowing money and never repaying it.
etymology: From Scots feck, 'effect, value', shortened from effect, plus -less.

definition: Highly fertile; able to produce abundant growth, offspring, or ideas.
examples: The river valley's fecund soil made it the region's best farmland.
She had a fecund imagination that produced a new story idea each morning.
etymology: From Latin fecundus, 'fruitful'.

definition: Showing very strong, passionate, and sincere feeling.
examples: She is a fervent supporter of the local team and never misses a game.
They made a fervent plea for help as the flood waters rose.
etymology: From Latin fervens, 'boiling, glowing', from fervere 'to boil'.

definition: Changing often and unpredictably, especially in loyalty or affection.
examples: The fickle crowd cheered him one week and booed him loudly the next.
Spring weather in the mountains is famously fickle, so pack for both sun and snow.
etymology: From Old English ficol, 'deceitful, treacherous'.

definition: Shockingly obvious and done openly without shame.
examples: The referee ejected him from the game immediately for a flagrant foul on the goalkeeper.
It was a flagrant violation of the privacy rules, and nobody tried to hide it.
etymology: From Latin flagrare, 'to blaze, burn', so 'blazing' into view.

definition: Courage and strength of mind in the face of pain or hardship.
examples: She faced her long recovery with quiet fortitude and never once complained to her nurses.
It took real fortitude to start over in a new country without family nearby.
etymology: From Latin fortitudo, 'strength', from fortis 'strong'.

definition: Happening by lucky chance, usually with a pleasant result.
examples: A fortuitous meeting at the airport led to their business partnership.
It was fortuitous that the plumber lived next door when the pipe burst.
etymology: From Latin fortuitus, 'happening by chance', from fors 'chance'.

definition: To encourage the growth or development of something over time.
examples: Good teachers foster curiosity by welcoming every question.
The festival aims to foster understanding between neighboring communities.
etymology: From Old English fostrian, 'to nourish, bring up', related to foda, 'food'.

definition: Not serious or sensible; silly or of little real value.
examples: He spent his bonus on frivolous gadgets he never used.
The judge dismissed the frivolous lawsuit within minutes, calling it a waste of court time.
etymology: From Latin frivolus, 'silly, worthless'.

definition: Careful about spending money and avoiding waste.
examples: Growing up poor made her frugal, and she still reuses every jar.
A frugal traveler, he packed his own lunches and stayed in hostels.
etymology: From Latin frugalis, 'economical', from frugi 'useful, thrifty'.

definition: Excessively flattering or effusive, to the point of seeming insincere.
examples: The senator's fulsome praise for the donors made the whole room cringe.
I distrust fulsome compliments from people who stand to gain something from me.
etymology: From Middle English ful 'full' + -some; it originally meant abundant, later 'excessive' and insincere.

definition: Having no chance of success; pointless.
examples: Their futile attempts to start the old car ended with a dead battery.
It is futile to argue with someone who refuses to listen.
etymology: From Latin futilis, 'leaky, worthless', related to fundere 'to pour'.

definition: Talking a great deal, especially about unimportant things.
examples: My garrulous neighbor can turn a quick hello into an hour-long monologue.
The garrulous cab driver told us his entire life story before we reached the airport.
etymology: From Latin garrulus, 'talkative', from garrire 'to chatter'.

definition: Using pompous, lofty language to impress others.
examples: The grandiloquent speaker buried a simple idea under layers of ornate phrases.
His grandiloquent toast went on so long that the champagne went flat.
etymology: From Latin grandiloquus, from grandis 'great' + loqui 'to speak'.

definition: Unnecessary and done without good reason, often in an offensive way.
examples: Critics complained about the gratuitous violence in the new film, which added nothing to the story.
His gratuitous insult at the meeting helped no one and embarrassed the whole team.
etymology: From Latin gratuitus, 'freely given', from gratia 'favor'.

definition: Fond of company and enjoying being around other people.
examples: A gregarious host, he loved filling his house with friends every weekend.
Wolves are gregarious animals that live and hunt in packs.
etymology: From Latin gregarius, 'of a flock', from grex 'flock, herd'.

definition: Extremely tiring and demanding, requiring great effort over a long time.
examples: The grueling hike left everyone too exhausted to speak at dinner.
Medical residents endure grueling shifts that can last thirty hours.
etymology: From gruel, in the older phrase 'to give someone their gruel', meaning to punish or exhaust.

definition: Clever and sly skill in deceiving others to get what you want.
examples: The fox in the fable won the cheese through sheer guile.
He used guile rather than force to talk his way past security.
etymology: From Old French guile, 'deceit', of Germanic origin.

definition: Overused and lacking freshness, so that it has become dull.
examples: The movie was full of hackneyed lines we had heard a thousand times.
Avoid hackneyed openings like 'It was a dark and stormy night'.
etymology: From the English town name Hackney, whose horses were hired out, hence 'common, overused'.

definition: Denoting a past time that was idyllically happy and peaceful.
examples: She often recalled the halcyon summers she spent at her grandparents' lake house.
Those halcyon days before smartphones felt slower and somehow kinder.
etymology: From Greek halkyon, a mythical kingfisher said to calm the seas while nesting.

definition: To make progress or movement difficult by getting in the way.
examples: Heavy snow will hamper rescue efforts in the mountain region tonight.
A lack of funding continues to hamper research into the rare disease.
etymology: From Middle English hampren, of uncertain origin.

definition: A sign that something is about to happen.
examples: The first robin of the year is traditionally seen as a harbinger of spring.
Falling sales proved a harbinger of deeper trouble ahead for the struggling company.
etymology: From Old French herbergeor, 'one who provides lodging', later an advance messenger.

definition: Arrogantly proud and acting as if better than other people.
examples: The haughty waiter looked down his nose at our simple order.
She gave a haughty sniff and walked past the line of waiting guests.
etymology: From Old French haut, 'high', from Latin altus.

definition: Dominant influence or control by one state or group over others.
examples: For decades, one superpower's hegemony shaped the rules of global trade.
Critics argue the tech giants have established a hegemony over online advertising.
etymology: From Greek hegemonia, 'leadership', from hegemon 'leader'.

definition: To slow down or make it hard for something to happen.
examples: Poor lighting can hinder your ability to read safely at night.
Don't let fear of failure hinder you from trying something new.
etymology: From Old English hindrian, 'to hold back', related to 'behind'.

definition: Overly theatrical or dramatic in manner, as if for effect.
examples: His histrionic sighs and eye-rolls disrupted the quiet meeting.
The toddler's histrionic collapse in the cereal aisle drew sympathetic looks from other parents.
etymology: From Latin histrionicus, 'of an actor', from histrio 'actor'.

definition: To sharpen or refine a skill, ability, or tool through practice.
examples: She spent the summer working to hone her public speaking.
You can hone a knife in minutes with the right stone.
etymology: From Old English han, 'stone', originally a whetstone used to sharpen blades.

definition: Excessive pride and self-confidence that often leads to downfall.
examples: The CEO's hubris blinded him to the warning signs, and the company soon collapsed.
In Greek tragedy, hubris almost always brings a hero to ruin.
etymology: From Greek hybris, meaning 'insolence, outrage'.

definition: A person who attacks cherished beliefs or traditions.
examples: The young chef was an iconoclast who ignored every classic recipe.
As an iconoclast, she delighted in challenging the art world's rules.
etymology: From Greek eikonoklastes, 'image breaker', from eikon 'image' + klan 'to break'.

definition: A peculiar habit or quirk that is distinctive to one person.
examples: His favorite idiosyncrasy was eating dessert before dinner, which delighted every child he met.
Every old house has its own idiosyncrasy, like a door that never quite shuts.
etymology: From Greek idiosynkrasia, from idios 'own' + syn 'together' + krasis 'mixture'.

definition: Extremely peaceful, happy, and picturesque, like a perfect pastoral scene.
examples: They spent an idyllic week in a cottage by the sea.
The village looked idyllic, with its stone bridge and flower-filled windowsills.
etymology: From idyll, from Greek eidyllion, a short poem about rural life.

definition: Causing public shame or disgrace; deeply humiliating.
examples: The team suffered an ignominious defeat, losing by fifty points at home.
His ignominious exit from office followed months of scandal.
etymology: From Latin ignominiosus, from ig- 'not' + nomen 'name, reputation'.

definition: A confusing, embarrassing, and tangled situation or disagreement.
examples: The budget imbroglio left the city council arguing for weeks.
What began as a small billing error became a legal imbroglio involving three companies.
etymology: From Italian imbrogliare, 'to tangle', borrowed into English in the 18th century.

definition: Treating all sides fairly, without favoring one over another.
examples: A judge must remain impartial and weigh the evidence from both sides.
We hired an impartial expert to settle the dispute between the neighbors.
etymology: From im- 'not' + partial, from Latin pars 'part, side'.

definition: A situation in which no progress is possible because of disagreement.
examples: Talks reached an impasse when neither side would agree to compromise on wages.
The two designers hit an impasse over the logo's color.
etymology: From French impasse, 'blind alley', from im- 'not' + passer 'to pass'.

definition: Perfect and without any fault or mistake.
examples: Her impeccable manners impressed everyone at the formal dinner, even the strictest guests.
The tailor delivered an impeccable suit that fit like a second skin.
etymology: From Latin impeccabilis, 'not liable to sin', from in- 'not' + peccare 'to sin'.

definition: Having little or no money, usually habitually.
examples: The impecunious student lived on instant noodles and borrowed textbooks.
Though impecunious, the young poet refused to take a job that bored him.
etymology: From im- 'not' + Latin pecunia 'money', itself linked to pecus 'cattle'.

definition: Not allowing something to pass through or affect it.
examples: The new jacket is completely impervious to rain and wind, even in a storm.
He seemed impervious to criticism and just kept working on his project each day.
etymology: From Latin impervius, from in- 'not' + pervius 'passable'.

definition: Acting quickly and rashly without stopping to think.
examples: His impetuous decision to quit on the spot surprised even his friends.
The impetuous young knight charged ahead before the others were ready.
etymology: From Latin impetuosus, 'violent', from impetus 'attack, rush'.

definition: Unable to be calmed or satisfied, and relentless in opposition.
examples: She was an implacable opponent who never gave an inch.
The implacable storm kept the ferries in port for three days.
etymology: From Latin implacabilis, from in- 'not' + placare 'to soothe'.

definition: Suggested or understood without being stated directly.
examples: There was an implicit warning in her calm tone of voice.
Employees have an implicit understanding that emails should be answered quickly.
etymology: From Latin implicitus, 'entangled', past participle of implicare 'to enfold'.

definition: Done without preparation or planning, on the spur of the moment.
examples: The band gave an impromptu concert on the sidewalk.
He made an impromptu speech when the guest of honor was delayed.
etymology: From French impromptu, from Latin in promptu, 'in readiness'.

definition: To challenge the truth, honesty, or integrity of something or someone.
examples: The defense lawyer tried to impugn the witness's credibility.
I don't mean to impugn your motives, but the numbers don't add up.
etymology: From Latin impugnare, 'to attack', from in- 'against' + pugnare 'to fight'.

definition: Only just begun and not yet fully formed or developed.
examples: Her inchoate plans for a bakery were still just sketches on a napkin.
He felt an inchoate unease he could not yet put into words.
etymology: From Latin inchoare, 'to begin', originally a term for starting work.

definition: Clear, sharp, and direct in thought or expression.
examples: Her incisive question exposed the flaw in the plan at once.
The columnist is known for incisive commentary on city politics.
etymology: From Latin incisivus, 'cutting', from incidere 'to cut into'.

definition: Out of place or not fitting with its surroundings.
examples: A neon sign looked incongruous on the ancient stone wall.
It seemed incongruous to see a tuxedo at a beach cleanup.
etymology: From Latin incongruus, from in- 'not' + congruus 'agreeing'.

definition: Persisting tirelessly without ever seeming to grow weary.
examples: The indefatigable volunteer worked every shift through the entire flood relief effort.
Her indefatigable curiosity kept her reading well past midnight.
etymology: From Latin indefatigabilis, from in- 'not' + de- + fatigare 'to tire'.

definition: Impossible to erase or forget, like a stain or memory.
examples: The trip left an indelible mark on her view of the world.
He wore an indelible grin after hearing the good news.
etymology: From Latin indelebilis, from in- 'not' + delere 'to destroy'.

definition: Habitually lazy and unwilling to make any effort.
examples: The indolent cat spent the whole day stretched out on the sunny windowsill.
His indolent attitude toward homework worried his teachers and frustrated his parents all year.
etymology: From Latin indolens, 'feeling no pain', from in- 'not' + dolere 'to suffer'.

definition: Too great or deep to be put into words.
examples: She felt an ineffable joy as the sun rose over the mountain.
The ineffable beauty of the music moved the audience to tears.
etymology: From Latin ineffabilis, from in- 'not' + effari 'to speak out'.

definition: Certain to happen and impossible to avoid.
examples: With so many problems, the company's collapse seemed inevitable.
Change is inevitable, so it helps to learn to adapt early.
etymology: From Latin inevitabilis, 'unavoidable', from in- 'not' + evitare 'to avoid'.

definition: Impossible to stop or change, continuing relentlessly.
examples: The inexorable rise of sea levels is a growing threat to many coastal towns.
He felt the inexorable pull of home after years abroad.
etymology: From Latin inexorabilis, from in- 'not' + exorare 'to move by entreaty'.

definition: Innocent, honest, and trusting, without any hidden motives.
examples: The ingenuous child told the guests exactly what she thought.
His ingenuous smile made it hard to stay angry with him.
etymology: From Latin ingenuus, 'native, freeborn, frank'.

definition: Existing as a natural, permanent, or essential part of something.
examples: Some risk is inherent in any investment, no matter how careful you are.
She believed in the inherent goodness of most people.
etymology: From Latin inhaerens, 'sticking to', from in- 'in' + haerere 'to stick'.

definition: Harmful or hostile in effect; tending to obstruct or damage.
examples: Constant noise is inimical to deep concentration.
Policies inimical to small businesses drove many owners out of the downtown area.
etymology: From Late Latin inimicalis, from Latin inimicus 'enemy'.

definition: Present from birth as a natural part of one's character.
examples: She has an innate sense of rhythm that no lesson could teach.
Babies show an innate preference for looking at human faces.
etymology: From Latin innatus, 'inborn', from in- 'in' + nasci 'to be born'.

definition: Harmless and unlikely to offend or cause trouble.
examples: It seemed an innocuous comment, yet it started an argument.
The spider looked scary but is entirely innocuous to humans.
etymology: From Latin innocuus, from in- 'not' + nocuus 'harmful'.

definition: Lacking flavor, interest, or excitement, and so dull or bland.
examples: The soup was so insipid that everyone reached for the salt.
Critics dismissed the film as an insipid romance with no spark.
etymology: From Latin insipidus, from in- 'not' + sapidus 'savory'.

definition: Showing a casual, cheerful lack of concern or worry.
examples: He strolled in an hour late with an insouciant grin.
Her insouciant attitude toward deadlines drove her manager to despair.
etymology: From French insouciant, from in- 'not' + soucier 'to care'.

definition: Narrow-minded and uninterested in ideas or people from outside one's own group.
examples: The insular village distrusted anyone who had not been born there.
An insular mindset can keep a company from noticing new competitors.
etymology: From Latin insularis, 'of an island', from insula 'island'.

definition: Strong honesty and adherence to moral principles, even when unobserved.
examples: A person of integrity admits mistakes instead of blaming other people.
The scandal damaged the integrity of the entire institution and its leaders.
etymology: From Latin integritas, 'wholeness', from integer 'whole, untouched'.

definition: Destructive to both sides, especially of conflict within a group.
examples: Internecine feuding among the founders nearly destroyed the startup.
The party was weakened by internecine battles over who would lead it.
etymology: From Latin internecinus, 'deadly', from inter- + necare 'to kill'.

definition: Refusing to change one's position or compromise.
examples: The intransigent union leader rejected every offer the company put on the table.
Both parties stayed intransigent, and the strike dragged on for weeks.
etymology: From Spanish intransigente, from Latin in- 'not' + transigere 'to come to an agreement'.

definition: Fearless and adventurous, willing to face danger.
examples: The intrepid explorer crossed the desert alone on foot, carrying only water.
Two intrepid students volunteered to test the untried experiment first.
etymology: From Latin intrepidus, from in- 'not' + trepidus 'alarmed'.

definition: Understood or felt easily without needing conscious reasoning or instruction.
examples: The app has an intuitive layout that anyone can learn in minutes.
Good doctors often have an intuitive sense that something is wrong.
etymology: From Medieval Latin intuitivus, from Latin intueri 'to look at, consider'.

definition: To overwhelm with a huge number of things, or to flood with water.
examples: Fans will inundate the box office the moment tickets go on sale.
Heavy rain can inundate the low fields along the river.
etymology: From Latin inundare, 'to flood', from in- + unda 'wave'.

definition: Having a long-established habit or feeling that is unlikely to change.
examples: He is an inveterate gambler who can't walk past a casino.
My grandmother was an inveterate letter writer well into her nineties.
etymology: From Latin inveteratus, 'made old', from in- + vetus 'old'.

definition: Easily angered; prone to quick, sharp displays of temper.
examples: The irascible old chef threw spatulas whenever an order came out wrong.
Hunger made her irascible, so we stopped for lunch before anyone snapped.
etymology: From Latin irascibilis, from irasci 'to be angry', from ira 'anger'.

definition: Showing a lack of respect for things usually taken seriously.
examples: The comedian's irreverent jokes about politicians drew roars of laughter.
Her irreverent tone made the dull seminar much more fun.
etymology: From Latin irreverens, from in- 'not' + reverens 'respectful'.

definition: Naive, simplistic, or lacking in substance and maturity.
examples: The film's jejune dialogue made the serious plot hard to take seriously.
Her essay was jejune, offering slogans where it needed real analysis.
etymology: From Latin jejunus, 'fasting, meager'.

definition: Aggressive, boastful patriotism, especially favoring war with other countries.
examples: The newspaper's jingoism whipped the public into a frenzy before the war.
Politicians often resort to jingoism when they want to distract from problems at home.
etymology: From the 1870s British music-hall song containing the oath 'by jingo', supporting war with Russia.

definition: Cheerful, friendly, and full of good humor.
examples: The jovial innkeeper greeted us with a booming laugh and a warm meal.
Grandpa was in a jovial mood and told jokes all through dinner.
etymology: From French jovial, 'under the influence of Jupiter', associated with happiness in astrology.

definition: To place two things side by side to highlight their contrast.
examples: The exhibit will juxtapose old photographs with modern street scenes.
Poets often juxtapose joy and grief to make each feel sharper.
etymology: From French juxtaposer, from Latin juxta 'next to' + French poser 'to place'.

definition: Sharing a similar nature, spirit, or close relationship.
examples: At the conference she found kindred spirits who loved obscure poetry as much as she did.
The two novels have a kindred theme of loneliness in big cities.
etymology: From Old English cynn 'kin, family' + ræden 'condition'.

definition: Tearful, or tending to cause tears and sadness.
examples: The lachrymose ballad had half the audience dabbing their eyes.
He grew lachrymose after a second glass of wine and began recalling old loves.
etymology: From Latin lacrimosus, from lacrima 'tear'.

definition: Using very few words, often in a blunt way.
examples: His laconic reply to the long email was simply 'Fine'.
The laconic cowboy answered every question with a single nod.
etymology: From Greek Lakonikos, 'Spartan', as the Spartans were known for brief speech.

definition: A gap or missing part, especially in a text or body of knowledge.
examples: The historian noted a lacuna in the records covering the winter of 1347.
There is a glaring lacuna in the report: it never mentions the costs.
etymology: From Latin lacuna, 'pit, gap', related to lacus 'lake'.

definition: To express deep sadness or regret about something.
examples: Fans lament the closing of the old theater on Main Street.
She would often lament the days when neighbors knew each other well.
etymology: From Latin lamentari, 'to wail', from lamentum 'a weeping'.

definition: Slow, relaxed, and lacking energy, often in a pleasant way.
examples: They spent a languid afternoon drifting down the slow river with nothing to do.
She gave a languid wave and went back to her book.
etymology: From Latin languidus, from languere 'to be faint'.

definition: Generous giving of money or gifts, often by someone wealthy.
examples: The museum owes its new wing to the largesse of a local donor.
Students benefited from the largesse of an alumnus who funded scholarships.
etymology: From Old French largesse, from large 'generous'.

definition: Existing but not yet visible, active, or developed.
examples: The coach saw latent talent in the shy new player.
The virus can stay latent in the body for years.
etymology: From Latin latens, 'lying hidden', from latere 'to lie hidden'.

definition: Deserving praise and admiration, even if the result is imperfect.
examples: Her goal of cutting waste in the office is laudable.
It is laudable that so many neighbors volunteered after the storm.
etymology: From Latin laudabilis, from laudare 'to praise'.

definition: Extravagant, rich, and given in great and generous abundance.
examples: They threw a lavish party with live music and a five-course dinner.
The hotel's lavish lobby has marble floors and a giant crystal chandelier.
etymology: From Old French lavasse, 'downpour of rain', from laver 'to wash'.

definition: Skillful trickery or sleight of hand, used to deceive or impress.
examples: The magician's legerdemain made the coin vanish from his open palm.
Through accounting legerdemain, the company hid its losses for years.
etymology: From Old French leger de main, 'light of hand'.

definition: Gentle and merciful in punishment or in applying rules.
examples: The judge was lenient and gave the first-time offender a warning.
Our lenient teacher accepts late homework if you explain what happened.
etymology: From Latin leniens, 'soothing', from lenis 'soft, mild'.

definition: Sluggish and drowsy, with very little energy or desire to move.
examples: After the enormous lunch, the whole office felt lethargic and a little sleepy.
The patient seemed lethargic and slept through most of the day.
etymology: From Greek lethargos, 'forgetful', from lethe 'forgetfulness'.

definition: Humor or light-heartedness, especially when a situation is serious.
examples: A moment of levity eased the tension in the boardroom.
He rarely showed levity at work, which made his jokes surprising.
etymology: From Latin levitas, 'lightness', from levis 'light'.

definition: Very talkative, often to the point of rambling.
